title: The Answer Was on Top
pace_basis: same runtime-anchored pace paragraph as 2026-09-19 and 09-23 (1.907 wps measured)
note: Numbers and acronyms written phonetically for the synth; on screen they render as numerals. Every factual line carries a claim id.

lines.text: A Kodiak woman asked Google when snipe season opens.
It said September first.
So on September fifth she shot three snipe.
lines.display: So on September 5th she shot three snipe.

lines.text: But the wildlife trooper's report says the general season didn't open until October eighth.
lines.display: But the wildlife trooper's report says the general season didn't open until October 8th.

lines.text: So which page can a hunter trust?
At home she looked up the rules, saw her mistake, and called troopers to turn herself in.
That trooper ran her exact search. He got the same wrong answer.
So the wrong answer came back twice.
She pleaded no contest and paid a hundred fifty dollars.
lines.display: She pleaded no contest and paid $150.

lines.text: She told a reporter, I feel terrible.
Public Safety spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time A I has been cited. He expects more.
lines.display: Public Safety spokesman Austin McDaniel thinks it's the first time AI has been cited. He expects more.

lines.text: Weren't there warnings? There were.
Google's help page says A I answers may include mistakes. Check more than one place.
lines.display: Google's help page says AI answers may include mistakes. Check more than one place.

lines.text: Google didn't respond to the Alaska Beacon's request for comment.
McDaniel says the one source of truth is Fish and Game's regulations and emergency orders.
So she still paid. But that source has a catch.
Fish and Game's own page says its online regulations are simplified, and emergency orders can override them.
So it's summaries stacked on the law itself.
The answer was on top. What counts sits underneath.
Fish and Game will mail you the regulations.
Before you hunt, which page do you trust?
